newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: New party wins token opposition seat in Mauritania.
newsitem.headline: New party wins token opposition seat in Mauritania.

text.p: A new party championing the rights of Mauritania's blacks and ex-slaves or their descendants won the first opposition seat in the national assembly after a two-round legislative election dominated by the ruling party.
A week after the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party won a crushing majority amid cries of fraud, results in Friday's second round gave Action for Change one seat.

Former gendarme Kebe Abdoulaye, from the Moslem West African nation's black community, will represent Action for Change and the capital Nouakchott's Sebha district in the new assembly, the second since Mauritania's 1991 democratic transition.

The ruling party won all four other seats where Action for Change contested the second round, taking its tally so far in the 79-seat assembly to 67 -- the same as in a 1992 election boycotted by the opposition.

With announcements on eight seats still awaited on Saturday, independents had won three seats and a small party supporting President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya another one. A second woman still had a chance of winning.
Most independent candidates were ruling party supporters denied the party ticket. They alone were in the race against the ruling party for the remaining eight seats.

The election also gave Mauritania, a former French colony straddling Arab and black Africa, its first woman assembly member, from the Harratin -- Arabic-speaking ex-slaves -- and a member of the ruling party.
The October 11 first round was Mauritania's first truly multi-party legislative election.
The opposition boycotted the first such election in 1992, alleging widespread fraud after Taya, who seized power in a bloodless 1984 coup, won a six-year term.
Action for Change was the only opposition party represented in Friday's second round.

Veteran opposition stalwart Ahmed Ould Daddah, who alleged massive fraud in the first round, pulled his Union of Democratic Forces-New Era party out of the runoffs, passing up the chance of winning two seats in Nouakchott. The ruling party won both.

Action for Change, formed just over a year ago and led by former slave Messoud Ould Boulkheir, had the backing of Ould Daddah's party and the moderate Union for Democracy and Progress. Witnesses described turnout in the capital as low.
Mauritania, a sparsely populated nation of 2.2 million people, stands at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert.
Light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population and Harratin the remainder. Mauritania formally banned slavery in 1980.
International observers spoke of "imperfections" in the first round, in which the opposition had been hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998.

Rivalry between Moors and black Mauritanians spilled over into tension with neighbouring Senegal and bloodshed in 1989. Migrant Moors and Harratins were killed in race riots in Senegal and there were reprisal killings in Mauritania.
The rise of Action for Change has put the racial divide, which has plagued Mauritania since independence in 1960, firmly back on the agenda.
Politicians say that for the first time Harratin, who historically consider themselves part of the Arab community with the Moors, have made common cause with blacks from the south.
